chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Imran ibn Musa, and Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Regarding the man who prays, and in front of him is a Mushaf (Quran) open, in his Qiblah, he said: 'No.' I said, 'And if it is in a wrapping?' He said: 'Yes.'
And he said: 'The man cannot pray, and in his Qiblah is a fire, or iron.'

And regarding the man who prays, and in front of him is a hanging lantern and in it is fire, except that it is towards him. He said: 'When it is high, it would be evil. One should not pray towards it.'

key_terms.بِحِيَالِهِ: Facing him / in front of him
key_terms.مُصْحَفٌ: A codex or copy of the Quran

ai.seo_question: What objects in front of a worshipper invalidate or make prayer disliked in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the juristic nuances of the 'sutra' (prayer screen) concept, distinguishing between objects that invalidate prayer when placed directly in the Qiblah line, such as an open Quran, fire, or iron, and those that are merely disliked, like a high-hanging lantern. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on minimizing distractions and maintaining reverence during prayer, while allowing flexibility for wrapped scriptures. The ruling underscores the importance of visual focus (khushu) by removing potential obstructions or sources of distraction from the direct line of sight toward the Kaaba.
